rationale.answer_analysis: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, rapidly progressive, acquired demyelinating autoimmune disorder of the peripheral nervous system. It is characterized by ascending paralysis, often preceded by a viral or bacterial infection. The most life-threatening complication of GBS is respiratory failure due to paralysis of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Monitoring respiratory status is paramount. Key indicators of impending respiratory failure include a rapidly declining forced vital capacity (FVC), paradoxical breathing (abdominal wall moves inward on inspiration), accessory muscle use, increased work of breathing, and subjective reports of dyspnea or difficulty speaking in full sentences. A significant drop in FVC (e.g., below 20 mL/kg or 1.5-2 L in an adult) indicates severe respiratory muscle weakness and necessitates preparation for ventilatory support. While dysphagia and paresthesia are important GBS symptoms, respiratory compromise directly threatens life and requires the most immediate intervention. The nurse must continuously assess respiratory rate, depth, effort, oxygen saturation, and lung sounds, and be prepared to escalate care, including notifying the provider and preparing for intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Delay in any of these steps significantly increases mortality.
